title: How Thanksgiving Works
summary: Josh and Chuck talk about Thanksgiving history and myths. They open with casual banter about their favorite holidays and Chuck's love of Thanksgiving. They then cover the Pilgrims and Puritans at Plymouth (including the separate group called the Strangers), the harsh first winter and deaths, the abandoned Patuxet village, and Squanto's help teaching farming and survival. They discuss the 1621 harvest feast, Native American harvest celebrations and traditional foods, and the later King Philip's War. Next they cover how Sarah Josepha Hale's letter-writing campaign shaped the modern holiday, Lincoln's proclamation, and Franklin Roosevelt moving the holiday earlier for Christmas shopping ("Frank's Giving"). They discuss why turkey and pumpkin pie were probably not at the first feast, and the turkey-and-tryptophan sleepiness myth, including the calorie load of a typical meal. They close with football traditions (Detroit Lions, Dallas Cowboys, Macy's parade balloon inflation in New York) and cooking-time tips.

segments.title: Opening banter and favorite holidays
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck joke around and discuss which holiday each likes best, with Chuck naming Thanksgiving.

segments.title: Myths about the Pilgrims and the first Thanksgiving
segments.summary: They say school pageant depictions are partly accurate but wrong on clothing, such as buckles, which came later. They introduce the Puritans and the Strangers who settled Plymouth together.

segments.title: Harsh first winter at Plymouth
segments.summary: The colonists arrived in November, and in the first months about 48 of the original 100 died. The survivors were poorly prepared, and they brought grain that would not grow in North America.

segments.title: Patuxet village and Squanto
segments.summary: The settlers found the deserted Patuxet village, emptied by smallpox brought by English explorers and traders. Squanto, who had been taken to England, returned to find the settlers starving and helped them survive by teaching farming, hunting, shellfish harvesting, and maple sugaring.

segments.title: The 1621 feast and Native harvest traditions
segments.summary: The feast that followed was held in the fall, possibly sponsored by the Wampanoag, and was probably based on Native foods. They discuss traditional Native dishes and Native harvest celebrations, and note that the Wampanoag celebrated more often than the Puritans did. They also say the later King Philip's War ended the peace.

segments.title: Sarah Hale, Lincoln, and Roosevelt's date change
segments.summary: They cover how George Washington's sporadic proclamations, Sarah Hale's letter campaign, and Lincoln's proclamation shaped the holiday. Franklin Roosevelt moved it a week earlier to extend Christmas shopping, which led to the nickname Frank's Giving.

segments.title: Turkey and pumpkin pie at the first feast
segments.summary: They argue that turkey was probably not served at the first feast, which likely included venison, fowl, ducks, geese, and cranberries. They also say pumpkin pie was impossible at the first feast because there was no flour, milk, or working oven.

segments.title: Tryptophan myth and calories of the meal
segments.summary: They explain that tryptophan in turkey is not really the cause of sleepiness. The large calorie and fat load of the meal, about 3,000 calories and 29 grams of fat, is more likely responsible, and it would take hours of running to burn off.

segments.title: Thanksgiving football and the Macy's parade
segments.summary: They discuss the football tradition, including the Detroit Lions playing on Thanksgiving since 1934 and the Dallas Cowboys joining later. They also recommend watching the Macy's parade balloons being inflated in New York City.

segments.title: Turkey cooking times and sign-off
segments.summary: Chuck and Josh give turkey cooking time guidance for stuffed and unstuffed birds, urge listeners to give thanks and remember the vanquished, and close the episode.
